title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: what would you make a world out of? the Purusha Sukta's answer is an offering, with the seasons as its ingredients

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's proportion: all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.

What would you make a world out of? Clay, shaped by a potter's hands, is one answer. A spoken word is another. A seed, a shell, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way. The Purusha Sukta's answer comes from the fire ritual the hymn itself describes, where offerings are poured into a flame. In this hymn the world comes from an offering, and the ingredients aren't butter and wood. They're spring, summer and autumn.
screen: `CLAY? A WORD? A SEED?` → `THE HYMN'S ANSWER: AN OFFERING.` → `THE INGREDIENTS ARE SEASONS.`

segments.voice: The word is yajna, a sacrifice, an offering poured into fire in Vedic worship. Verse six says that when the gods performed a yajna with the Purusha as the offering, spring was its melted butter, summer its fuel, autumn the offering itself. A fire ritual where the seasons are what's poured in: the year itself, burning as an offering. Verse seven: on the sacred grass they sprinkled him, the one born in the beginning, and the gods and the seers offered with him. From that offering, fully given, came the creatures of the air, the forest and the village. Verse nine turns the hymn back on itself. From that offering were born the verses and the chants, the meters, the sacrificial formulas: the Vedas themselves, the very kind of text the hymn belongs to. A hymn telling where hymns come from. Verse ten adds horses, cattle, goats and sheep. Readers take this offering in different ways. Some traditional readers treat it as a sacred pattern for the fire rituals that followed: what the gods did first, priests repeat. Others read it more inwardly, as the one becoming the many by giving itself away. Either way, in this telling the world isn't built from outside, like a house. It comes from something given, and what comes from it, the songs, the animals, the seasons, carries the mark of that giving.
screen: `YAJNA: AN OFFERING INTO FIRE.` · `SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN: THE INGREDIENTS.` · `FROM IT: CREATURES, CHANTS AND VERSES.` · `A WORLD THAT COMES FROM GIVING.`

segments.voice: Notice the season where you are, the light, the air, the temperature on your skin, and bring to mind one thing it has given you lately: a cool morning, a long evening, fruit, rain. On each out-breath, let it go the way something is poured into a fire, not lost but given; if you pray, make the out-breath an offering, and if not, let each breath out be a small giving.
The Purusha Sukta. In its middle verses, the gods offer the Purusha, with spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it come creatures, chants and verses.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. In this hymn, even the chants are born from a giving. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindu households and temples keep the practice of offering into fire, and the Purusha Sukta is among the Vedic hymns recited in worship, where its picture of the first offering is remembered.

notes: Paraphrase of 10.90.6–10 from memory; confirm order. 6: vasanto asyāsīd ājyaṃ grīṣma idhmaḥ śarad dhaviḥ. 7: on the barhis (sacred grass), the gods, sādhyas and ṛṣis offered. 8: from the sacrifice the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) was gathered; animals of air, forest and village. 9: ṛcaḥ, sāmāni, chandāṃsi, yajus. 10: horses, those with two rows of teeth, cows, goats and sheep.
The hook's 'clay, a spoken word, a seed, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way' lists creation images without naming or comparing any tradition. Confirm it reads as neutral.
The hymn does not describe violence in detail; the script keeps to 'offering' and does not dwell on the Purusha as victim. Confirm tone.
'A fire was kept and offerings were poured into it' describes Vedic household practice generally; confirm.
